messages.subject: Binomial models
parts:
Hi All,

Quick question. I am interested in applying a binomial distance model wit=
h a normal key detection function to a large dataset of bird point count =
surveys where observers have tallied counts into two intervals: 0-50 m an=
d >51 m. However for the latter interval, half of the data were collected=
to an unlimited distance and the other half to 150 m. I'm curious as to=
whether it is valid to applied the binomial model to truncated data. Bu=
ckland (1987:382) seems to indicate that the binomial model cannot be app=
lied to truncated data but I am curious whether ideas on this matter have=
changed in the intervening years. Thanks in advance for your help.

Sincerely,

Steve Matsuoka

Lit. Cited
Buckland. 1987. On the variable circular plot method of estimating animal=
density. Biometrics 43:363-384.

messages.author: d718c6bb1db28db2
messages.subject: Re: Binomial models
parts:
Steve, no reason at all why you shoudn't fit a binomial model to
truncated data - you can do that in Distance. However, the binomial
models in my 1987 paper are for untruncated data, and the analytic
estimators given there shouldn't be used for truncated data.

Steve Buckland

> > Quick question. I am interested in applying a binomial distance model with a normal key detection function to a large dataset of bird point count surveys where observers have tallied counts into two intervals: 0-50 m and>51 m. However for the latter interval, half of the data were collected to an unlimited distance and the other half to 150 m. I'm curious as to whether it is valid to applied the binomial model to truncated data. Buckland (1987:382) seems to indicate that the binomial model cannot be applied to truncated data but I am curious whether ideas on this matter have changed in the intervening years. Thanks in advance for your help.
